h1: On paper the power fell short. The nameplates said otherwise.
description: A corner restaurant unit on New York Avenue, DC, matched to a national brand's format: power, plant and access read from the building itself.
summary: A national food and beverage brand was considering a corner restaurant unit in an Art-Deco office building on New York Avenue. The question wasn't whether the space was good. It was what their format would need from it, and what the space already had to give. One visit answered that.

findings.title: The service was bigger than the brand needed. One transformer was the only gap.
findings.body: The unit has a 400 A service at 480 V, which is more capacity than the brand's standard asks for, and the panel directory showed plenty of spare ways. Everything at 208 V passes through a single step-down transformer sized for the previous use, and reading its rating plate is what pinned that down.
findings.action: A larger step-down transformer and a new 208 V board, fed from the spare capacity already there. A far smaller job than a new utility service.

photos.alt: Dry-type step-down transformer in the electrical room with its rating plate
photos.caption: The step-down transformer, read from its plate.

findings.title: A full kitchen exhaust system the new format doesn't need.
findings.body: The space carries a complete, ducted, roof-discharging kitchen hood with fire suppression and a dedicated plant room, all maintained and in service. The brand's format needs none of it. Taking it out frees floor area and a plant room on a compact unit, and clears the gas load entirely.
findings.action: Plan the decommissioning into the fit-out, and confirm which items belong to the outgoing tenant or an equipment lessor before anything is removed.

photos.alt: Stainless steel kitchen hood canopy with fire suppression nozzles
photos.caption: Hood canopy with its suppression nozzles.

findings.title: A door straight into a manned office lobby, and the building's own heating and cooling.
findings.body: The unit opens directly into the building's lobby, so it draws office footfall as well as street trade. It is also served by the base building's heating and chilled water, so there is no rooftop equipment to replace and no roof access to negotiate.
findings.action: Treat the lobby door as a second frontage in the layout, and confirm the terminal unit's duty with the building engineer during design.

photos.alt: Art-Deco office building lobby corridor with terrazzo floor
photos.caption: The building lobby the unit opens onto.

also: We also identified the original 2007 permit set as this space, which gave the design team a reliable base drawing from day one, and traced the mechanical, electrical and plumbing sheets that weren't in the pack to a simple records request.
delivered: Within the week, the client had a narrative report, a 3D walkthrough, a nameplate-level equipment register and a fit-out plan matched to their brand standards.

In one visit we traced the electrical allocation back to the base-building switchboard in the cellar, read every pipe label and nameplate in the space, opened the wall chases, followed the planned utility routes on the level below and captured the whole shell in 360. kicker: Cold shell, stripped to structure · New York, NY · Surveyed September 2026
h1: An empty shell on Fifth Avenue, with more already in it than the brief said.
description: A cold shell retail space on Fifth Avenue, New York, surveyed for a national brand: spare power, labeled pipework and a waste stack found in one visit.
summary: A growing café chain was looking at a ground-floor cold shell in a Midtown office tower, a few steps from Fifth Avenue. The leasing brief said there was no MEP at all, with utilities to be brought up from the level below. The brand needed to know what a first fit-out would really involve. One visit showed the starting point was a good deal further along than the paperwork suggested.

findings.title: The power was already waiting in the cellar. Twice over.
findings.body: Two spare 200 A, 480 V fused switches on the building's main switchboard are allocated to the space. The brand's standard of 400 A at 208 V works out to about 173 A at 480 V, so one switch covers the whole requirement and the second is headroom. Reading the switchboard labels in the cellar is what turned a line in a leasing email into a number the design team could use.
findings.action: Two 75 kVA step-down transformers, one on each switch, and a 480 V feeder up from the cellar. Agree where the transformers sit early, before the layout is fixed.

photos.alt: Blue base-building switchboard with a 200 A, 480 V fused switch and its feeder label
photos.caption: One of the two spare 200 A switches, read at the switchboard.

findings.title: The brief said condenser water. The pipe labels said there was more.
findings.body: At high level inside the space, a five-pipe bank carries the building's own markers: drain, condenser water supply and return, and a dual-temperature supply and return. That second pair is the building's changeover heating and cooling loop, and it was not in the brief. For a format that wants two zones of heating and cooling, it is a better starting point than condenser water alone.
findings.action: Ask the landlord which loops the tenant may use, and at what capacity, before the HVAC design starts. The space has one street elevation, so agree the outside-air and exhaust routes at the same time.

photos.alt: Five insulated pipes at high level with green markers reading drain, condenser water and dual temp supply and return
photos.caption: The labeled five-pipe services bank.

photos.alt: Stripped retail shell with exposed concrete beams and ductwork, looking toward the glazed storefront
photos.caption: The shell, looking toward the storefront.

findings.title: A waste stack inside the wall, not two floors of coring away.
findings.body: A built-out section of the demising wall looked like it was hiding pipework. Behind a hinged access door we found a cast-iron stack with cleanouts, plus domestic-size piping, rising through the floor. The planned water and waste route from the level below is also there and documented, so the plumbing design now has two options to choose from.
findings.action: Ask the landlord to confirm the stack's size and service and whether the tenant may connect to it. Get the slab thickness at any core locations before pricing the plumbing.

photos.alt: Open access panel showing a cast-iron stack with round cleanouts and smaller pipes and conduit
photos.caption: Behind the access door: the stack and its cleanouts.

also: A sprinkler main with heads already runs through the space, and the cellar riser carries a valved feed tagged for future first-floor retail. The brand's format needs no hood, no gas and no grease interceptor, which suits a cold shell that has none of them.
delivered: The client received a narrative report with a brand-standards gap analysis, two 360 walkthrough videos of the shell and the utility route below it, and a nameplate-level equipment register.

h1: Never occupied, but built with a food tenant in mind.
description: A never-occupied retail shell on Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA, surveyed for a national brand: capped water, vent and air provisions traced to the drawings.
summary: An expanding food and beverage operator was considering a ground-floor retail suite beside a building's main entrance on Berkeley Way. The space had never been occupied, and at first glance there was nothing in it: no lighting, no power, no restrooms. The brand needed to know how far a fit-out would have to start from zero. One visit, and the record drawings read on site, showed the shell had been planned for a food tenant from the start.

findings.title: A tall, bright, empty room with glass on two sides.
findings.body: The suite is about 45 by 37 feet under an exposed concrete waffle deck nearly 18 feet up, with tall double-glazed windows to the street, clerestory glazing above, and a glazed wall onto the building lobby. The polished concrete floor is flat and good enough to keep as a finished floor. Nothing has to be stripped out before work starts.
findings.action: Use the height and the lobby glazing in the layout, and treat the polished slab as a finish rather than something to cover.

photos.alt: Empty retail shell with tall storefront windows, clerestory glazing and a polished concrete floor
photos.caption: The storefront wall from inside the shell.

findings.title: Water, waste, air and heat were all capped and waiting.
findings.body: Labeled heating hot water and domestic cold water run through the space, with valved copper stubs and a capped supply-air trunk. The record drawings, photographed on site, show a 2-inch cold water stub for future retail, which beats the brand's 1½-inch standard, a capped 3-inch vent and waste provision, supply air balanced to 600 CFM, and make-up air and exhaust louver provisions in the envelope.
findings.action: Design the plumbing and ventilation around the provisions already there, and confirm stub locations and sizes on site as the first step of design.

photos.alt: Insulated pipes labeled heating hot return, heating hot supply and domestic cold water beside a capped supply-air duct
photos.caption: Labeled heating and cold water runs beside the capped supply-air trunk.

findings.title: A clean tenant panel on the wall. The allocation behind it was the one question left.
findings.body: In the rear service area sits a 150 A, 208 V tenant panel with all 42 spaces still blanked off. What the panel lacked was paperwork: how much of the building's capacity is set aside for this suite was not recorded on site. The suite next door gave a clear template, with a 480 V feed through a 112.5 kVA transformer to a 400 A board.
findings.action: Ask the landlord to confirm the feed to the panel and the capacity reserved for the suite, using the neighboring setup as the reference, before sizing any equipment.

photos.alt: Open grey tenant electrical panel with all branch spaces blanked and a 150 A main breaker
photos.caption: The unused 150 A tenant panel.

also: The record drawings also show a 3-inch gas provision to the future retail spaces, which the brand does not need but which adds to the suite's value. Building restrooms and showers sit directly behind the rear wall, so drainage runs are short.
delivered: The client received a narrative report, a register of every service provision found in the shell, and the full photo record organized by system.

findings.action: Confirm the rooftop unit's plate through the landlord's mechanical contractor, then plan the combined store's zoning around equipment already in place.

photos.alt: Rooftop HVAC plant with heat pump, condenser and exhaust fan on a mall roof
photos.caption: Tenant plant on the mall roof.

findings.title: Already half-joined, with a frontage on the street and one on the mall.
findings.body: The two suites already share a back of house, so the merge follows lines the building has drawn. The combined store gets a street arcade frontage and a mall concourse frontage. findings.action: Treat both frontages as entrances in the layout, and service and reuse the walk-in cooler rather than buy new.

photos.caption: The vacant suite, looking toward the street glazing.

h1: Two units, one future store, and the hookups already waiting in the shell.
description: Two mall units at Westfield Topanga, Canoga Park, combined for a national food and beverage brand: power, hot and chilled water and drainage confirmed.
summary: A national food and beverage brand was looking at two adjoining Level 1 units at Westfield Topanga, to be combined into one store of about 3,200 square feet. One unit was a former small retail shop, the other a bare landlord shell. The brand needed to know what arrives at the boundary: how much power, what heating and cooling, and where the drains connect. One visit answered all three.

findings.title: The existing service was sized for a small shop. The mall's switchboard has the room for more.
findings.body: The smaller unit runs on a 45 kVA transformer and a 100 A panel, which suited its last use but sits well short of the brand's 400 A standard. The larger unit had no service of its own yet. So we followed the feed back to the mall's main switchboard, where a 2,500 A-frame main breaker set at 2,000 A was carrying 165 A on a weekday afternoon. The capacity is there. The question is only the feeder.
findings.action: Ask the landlord for a 200 A feeder at 480 V and a 150 kVA step-down transformer in a new tenant electrical room. That delivers the brand's 400 A at 208 V and retires the old equipment.

photos.alt: Main service breaker in the mall switchboard with its ammeter display reading 165 amps
photos.caption: The mall's main breaker: 165 A on a 2,000 A setting.

findings.title: Hot and chilled water, already valved off for the next tenant.
findings.body: The mall runs on a central plant, so there are no rooftop units to inherit or replace. Inside the bare shell we found the building's four-pipe heating and chilled water mains, labeled, with a capped branch take-off, valves, a strainer and an energy meter kit already hanging on it for the future tenant. That gives the brand simultaneous heating and cooling without a single piece of new plant on a roof.
findings.action: Design four-pipe fan coils on the existing branch, to the landlord's chilled water criteria, and confirm the outside air and exhaust routes with the mall's engineering team.

photos.alt: Insulated hot and chilled water pipes with a capped branch take-off and blue-handled ball valves
photos.caption: The valved, capped branch left for the future tenant.

findings.title: A 16-foot concrete shell with drainage stubbed in the floor.
findings.body: Both units share a concrete pan-joist deck about 16 feet up, with the sprinkler mains already in place and slab floors level with the concourse. The landlord's 2021 underground plumbing sheet showed 4-inch waste and grease-waste stub-outs left for this space, and we matched them to a capped stub in the slab. On the landlord's own levels, gravity drainage can reach the far side of the combined store.
findings.action: Run the bar and dish area to the 4-inch grease-waste stub by gravity, keep the existing 1½-inch water service, and design the sprinklers off the mains as found.

photos.alt: Exposed concrete pan-joist deck over a mall shell unit with insulated water mains along the wall
photos.caption: The bare shell: concrete deck, sprinkler mains and the hydronic run.

also: The smaller unit's 1½-inch water service already meets the brand's standard, and the units have a rear exit into the mall's service corridor as well as frontage onto the lobby and the outdoor dining terrace.
delivered: Two days after the visit the client had a narrative report, a 3D scan, 360 walkthrough videos of both units and a nameplate-level equipment register, followed by a measured drawing set and Revit model.

findings.action: Carry the four units into the mechanical design as existing plant, confirm which gas meter serves the suite, and add heating and cooling to the warehouse only if the program needs it.

findings.title: The office layout was already most of a clinic.
findings.body: Ten perimeter offices, typically about 9'-6" to 10'-6" wide by 12' deep with 8'-5" ceilings, sit around a continuous hallway, each behind a glass front. Several fronts already carry frosted privacy film. For therapy rooms, the work is privacy, acoustics, finishes and lighting. The walls can stay where they are.

findings.body: Most rooms have full-width curtain-wall windows, which suits a calm therapy setting. findings.action: A landlord letter confirming the suite's share of power and cooling and the after-hours arrangements, and an early list of any dedicated circuits the clinic needs.

title: Animal Hospital Site Survey, Broadway, New York | Alturascope

kicker: Ground-floor retail shell · New York, NY · Surveyed August 2026
h1: The shell needed little. The questions were above and below it.
summary: A design-build contractor was pricing an animal hospital for a veterinary group in a vacant ground-floor retail unit on Broadway, just below Lincoln Square. An animal hospital needs far more plumbing, power and ventilation than a store, so the question was what the space could carry and where the cost really sat. stats.label: Slab to slab, back of house

findings.title: A 400 A panel was already on the wall. The fusing was the question.
findings.body: The unit has a 400 A, 208Y/120 V, 54-position panel in good order, and the new design keeps it. Reading the drawings against the nameplate showed the switch feeding it is fused at 300 A, while the design's own calculated demand comes to about 287 A. Workable, but close enough that it needed an answer before anyone put a number on the electrical package.
findings.action: Ask the engineer whether the intent is to re-fuse the existing switch to its full 400 A, and confirm the feeder route and length with the landlord before pricing.

photos.caption: The panel's nameplate: 400 A at 208Y/120 V.

findings.title: More than eight feet of room above the ceiling.
findings.body: We laser-measured the back of house at 18'-5" slab to slab. Under the new 10' ceiling that still leaves roughly 8'-5" of void, plenty for the new ductwork, the relocated water-source heat pumps, an energy recovery unit, medical gas piping and the hot water return. The heat pumps run on the building's condenser water loop, which we traced from labeled mains on the level below.
findings.action: Put the new plant in the back-of-house ceiling, where the room is, and confirm the condenser water capacity and billing with the landlord.

photos.alt: Clean back-of-house room with vinyl tile floor, gray doors and a red sprinkler riser
photos.caption: The back of house, where the new plant will sit.

findings.title: Inside, an easy box. The planning was in the slab.
findings.body: The previous fit-out was handed back clean, with a square grid, LED fixtures and no staining. The real scope was in the floor. The unit sits on an elevated slab over another occupied business, with homes above, so the new drainage for the hospital's sinks and fixtures runs below the slab in someone else's ceiling. That is normal for a ground-floor Manhattan unit, but it sets the program.
findings.action: Price the below-slab drainage and out-of-hours access as their own items, and build the landlord's coring approvals, scanning and notice periods into the program before the first core.

photos.caption: Front of house, handed back in good order.

h1: The frontage sold itself. The power took some detective work.
summary: A café brand was looking at a former café at the foot of an office building on Pennsylvania Avenue. The space looked right from the sidewalk. What they needed to know was how much of what sat behind the glass would carry over to their format, and what would still have to be added. One visit answered that.

findings.title: A double-height glass front on one of the city's best-known avenues.
findings.body: The unit sits in a fully glazed, double-height bay under a stainless entrance canopy, with double glazing throughout. Two upper windows, each about 9'9" wide by 8' high, give an elevated signage zone that reads from across the street. Inside, the trading area is roughly 41' by 35' and rises past 15', enough to set out a full bar layout without touching the structure.
findings.action: Make the two upper windows the primary branding zone, and plan the layout around the open trading floor as it stands.

photos.alt: Double-height aluminum curtain-wall storefront with a stainless entrance canopy
photos.caption: The double-height glazed bay and entrance canopy.

findings.title: Most of the costly infrastructure was already in place.
findings.body: The space is fully sprinklered, has two accessible restrooms, and is all-electric. Cooling comes from two water-source heat pumps on the building's condenser-water loop, twelve tons between them, and we matched both against the previous tenant's mechanical drawings. A grease interceptor installed in 2023 already covers a light-cooking menu. What is specific to the last café is its look: timber coffers, wallpaper and banquettes.

photos.caption: Inside the double-height window bay.

photos.caption: The previous café's coffered ceiling, part of the strip-out.

findings.title: The one number the building couldn't show us.

The brand's standard is 400 A, but its format draws far less than the hot-kitchen café the panels were sized for.
findings.action: Confirm the incoming figure from the building's electrical drawings or a clamp-meter reading before design, and check whether a 1½" water supply is available building-side (1" today).

It came fully fitted, with a long bar, a back-of-house kitchen and a walk-in cooler. h1: The power the café needed was already on a breaker. A steam boiler was using it.
description: A trading restaurant at Spectrum Center, Irvine, CA, surveyed for a café conversion: a power path without a service upgrade, found in one visit.
summary: A counter-service café brand was weighing a restaurant unit with a covered patio on the promenade at Spectrum Center. Its format runs blenders, espresso, refrigeration and ice, and the unit's 208 V panel was already close to its design load. The real question was whether the café would need a service upgrade at the center's shared switchboard. One visit, made while the restaurant was open and trading, showed it would not.

findings.title: The extra capacity was sitting behind the boiler breaker.
findings.body: The unit takes a 480 V supply through a 200 A switch, then steps down to a 208 V panel with a 125 A main and only about 10 A to spare. On the 480 V side, a 72 kW electric steam boiler the café has no use for sits on a 90 A breaker. A 75 kVA transformer draws almost exactly 90 A at 480 V and gives about 208 A at 208 V, and the existing 208 V panel already has a 225 A bus.
findings.action: Remove the boiler and reuse its breaker and feeder for a 75 kVA step-down transformer, with a larger main in the existing panel. That raises low-voltage capacity from about 125 A to about 200 A without touching the service. Confirm the feeder size and the existing transformer's plate during design.

photos.alt: Grey Eaton electrical panels and a small enclosure on a white back-of-house wall
photos.caption: The 208 V and 480 V panels in the back of house.

findings.title: Young plant that can stay.
findings.body: A 2022 Carrier packaged heat pump of about 10 tons serves the space, roughly 160 square feet per ton, which is more than a café's lighter cooking load needs. The walk-in cooler and freezer run on matched 2022 condensing units. The hood is protected by a UL-300 wet-chemical system tied into the center's fire alarm, the current standard and often a costly replacement in older restaurants.
findings.action: Keep the rooftop unit and both walk-ins as retained assets after a service visit, and take the grease line and second hood out. With less exhaust, the existing makeup air goes from tight to comfortable.

photos.alt: Red wet-chemical hood suppression cylinder with its release module and a stainless control panel
photos.caption: The UL-300 hood suppression system and its release.

findings.title: A covered patio that opens straight into the dining room.
findings.body: A six-panel folding door just over 15 feet tall opens the dining room onto a 395 square foot patio. The patio sits under a steel and timber canopy with radiant heaters and roller sunscreens on every bay. Inside, the dining ceiling is left open to the deck at about 15 and a half feet.
findings.action: Keep the folding doors, canopy, heaters and screens as the store's front, and confirm with the landlord whether the patio is part of the lease or licensed separately.

photos.alt: Timber joists and black steel beams of a patio canopy with pendant lights and hanging plants
photos.caption: The steel and timber patio canopy.

also: Water arrives through a 2-inch line, generous for a café of this size, and the gas meter is rated at 1,000 CFH, well beyond what the café would draw once the cook line goes. The center allows deliveries only before 10 AM, which we flagged for the operating plan.

kicker: Former restaurant shell · Sacramento, California · Surveyed July 2026
h1: A third of a big restaurant, with the whole building's capacity still behind it.
description: A former restaurant shell on J Street, Sacramento, surveyed for a café tenant: power, water, gas and ceiling heights confirmed in one pre-lease visit.
summary: A beverage-led café operator was considering about a third of a former full-service restaurant on J Street, in an early-1900s brick building in downtown Sacramento. The space had been taken back to shell and was about to be split into two tenancies, with the dividing wall not yet built. The questions were how much of the old restaurant's infrastructure a much smaller café could draw on, and what the new store would need of its own. One visit answered both, helped by a full set of as-built drawings we found on site.

findings.title: Utilities sized for a full restaurant, shared by two tenants.
findings.body: The tenant switchboard is a 1,200 A, 208 V board fed from a 2,000 A landlord board. The previous restaurant's calculated demand was about 990 A, so a café needing 400 A has plenty of room even after the split. A 3-inch water meter and a 7,000 CFH gas meter tell the same story. The original as-built drawings, which we found in the space, confirmed the capacities and filled in the panel schedules missing from the boards.
findings.action: Agree with the landlord how the switchboard, water and gas are divided between the two tenancies, and which basement services come with the café's demise. Keep the as-built drawing set with the project record.

photos.alt: Rear of an empty restaurant shell with board-formed concrete walls, columns and services under a steel deck
photos.caption: The rear of the shell, where services rise from the basement.

findings.title: Close to 16 feet at the front, and over 17 at the back.
findings.body: The front of house measures 15'-10" to its ceiling, under dark steel beams with corbelled brackets and white panels between them. The rougher rear half runs about 17 feet floor to ceiling, and 14'-10" to the underside of the concrete beams. There are no suspended ceilings anywhere, so the full height is usable for an open-ceiling concept.
findings.action: Plan the café's own new rooftop HVAC from the start, allowing for a crane lift on a building of this height, and keep the decorative front ceiling as part of the design.

photos.alt: Dark steel ceiling beams with corbelled brackets above tall divided-lite storefront windows
photos.caption: The decorative front-of-house ceiling and transom glazing.

findings.title: A period frontage with character worth keeping.
findings.body: The storefront is about 26'-9" wide, with 13 feet of glass and a divided-lite transom band that suits the building's age. Inside, a fine cast-plaster arched surround sits on the side wall, and much of the floor is an attractive terracotta mosaic tile that may be original to the building.
findings.action: Bring the arch and the mosaic floor into the design conversation early. Patch and make good the floor where the old kitchen's drains and penetrations come out, and decide whether to keep or replace the frontage railing.

photos.alt: Empty shell with a cast-plaster arched surround on a side wall, a mosaic tile floor and tall storefront glazing
photos.caption: The cast-plaster arch and the mosaic floor.

also: The building's sprinkler system is in an active maintenance program, and the basement holds hot-water plant from 2018 and 2019 and two walk-in boxes that could be reused if they come with the demise.
delivered: The client received a narrative building survey report with a nameplate-level equipment schedule and a 3D scan of the ground floor.

title: Café Unit Survey, Kierland Commons, Scottsdale | Alturascope
description: Pre-lease survey of a corner café unit at Kierland Commons, Scottsdale, AZ: all-electric, 480 V power, four heat pumps and water treatment in place.
kicker: Second-generation corner café unit · Scottsdale, Arizona · Surveyed June 2026
h1: No gas, four modern heat pumps, and power to spare.
summary: An expanding counter-service brand was looking at a trading corner café at Kierland Commons, with covered patio seating on three sides. Their format runs on electricity, water and refrigeration, so the question was how much of that was already in the building. We surveyed the unit while it was open for business, from the electrical room to the rooftop units. The answer was most of it, with a few things to confirm.

findings.title: The electrical backbone was already in place, with room to grow.
findings.body: The unit has a 480 V, three-phase service. A 112.5 kVA transformer steps it down to 208/120 V for equipment and lighting, which gives roughly 312 A on that side. The 480 V board serving the four rooftop heat pumps was carrying about 61 A of its 200 A. Those units date from 2018 to 2023 and give about 18 nominal tons across four zones, generous cooling for a glazed unit in the desert. We found no gas-fired equipment anywhere, which suits an all-electric format.
findings.action: Keep the distribution and re-circuit it to the new equipment. Confirm the exact spare capacity against a full circuit count, and run a cooling load check against the new layout.

photos.alt: Open-to-deck café ceiling with exposed spiral supply duct, round diffusers and pendant lights above tall storefront glazing
photos.caption: The open-to-deck dining room, with the supply ductwork on show.

findings.title: Water treatment, wet services and restrooms that carry over.
findings.body: The back of house holds a serviced treatment set: a twin-tank softener, a reverse-osmosis system and a booster pump, the kit a drinks bar needs. The bar position already has its supplies, drains, floor sinks and backflow devices. Two accessible restrooms are in good, recently styled condition. Grease is handled by a shared, building-scale interceptor in the rear service yard, so the brand may not need its own. The one gap is the water line, which is 1¼ inch against the brand's preferred 1½ inch, with the booster lifting the pressure.
findings.action: Check flow at peak demand before deciding on any upsize. Confirm the interceptor allocation with property management, and plan a light restroom refresh with an ADA check of mirror heights.

photos.alt: Accessible restroom with cream wall tile, a dark accent band, wall-hung basin, mirror and hand dryer
photos.caption: One of the two accessible restrooms.

findings.title: A shaded corner with a compact back room.
findings.body: A timber pergola with laser-cut metal screen panels wraps the frontage and both patio flanks, and the storefront is full-height glazing almost 16 feet wide in the main bay. Inside, the back of house is small and does a lot: warewashing, storage, refrigeration, the office and the IT rack share one L-shaped room of about 21 by 25 feet. Its lay-in tile ceiling makes services easy to rework. There is no walk-in cooler, but a rooftop condenser fed from the unit's own board could give a small cold room a head start.
findings.action: Treat back-of-house zoning as a real planning constraint from the first test-fit. Carry a refinish of the pergola timber in the exterior refresh.

photos.alt: Timber pergola with perforated metal screen panels against a blue sky, beside a stone pier
photos.caption: The pergola and screen panels over the patio.

title: Mall Food Court Unit Survey, Scottsdale, AZ | Alturascope
description: Pre-lease survey of a corner food-court unit at Scottsdale Fashion Square, AZ: 480 V power, fan-coils on the mall's water loop, walk-in and grease system.
kicker: Corner restaurant unit in an enclosed mall · Scottsdale, Arizona · Surveyed June 2026
h1: Two storefronts, no rooftop plant, and a building that does the cooling.
summary: A fast-casual food and drink operator was weighing a busy corner restaurant on the ground floor of Scottsdale Fashion Square. One side faces an open-air walkway with a patio, the other opens straight onto the food court. Deep inside a three-storey mall, the services work very differently from a standalone store. Over two days, with the unit trading, we traced each one back to where it comes from.

findings.title: Power arrives at 480 V, with three 208 V boards behind it.
findings.body: A single 480/277 V, three-phase service feeds a lightly loaded 150 A panel that serves the fan-coil units and a step-down transformer. The transformer in turn feeds three 208/120 V panels on 250 A frames, installed in 2010. On paper that is generous power for the incoming format. The transformer's rating plate was no longer readable, and its kVA is the number that sets the real ceiling on the 208 V side.
findings.action: Get the transformer rating from the building's records before the equipment layout is fixed. Everything else on the electrical side can be planned around it.

photos.alt: Two grey electrical panels on a white wall with conduit runs rising above them
photos.caption: Two of the 208/120 V panels in the back of house.

findings.title: The kitchen infrastructure was all there.
findings.body: The back of house has a built-in walk-in cooler of about 80 square feet, a Type I hood with wet-chemical suppression, and a large in-floor grease interceptor by the rear exit. Domestic water comes in at 1½ inch, which meets the brand's standard. Hot water is from a 2024 gas-fired storage heater, so natural gas is already at the unit, unlike the all-electric sites in the brand's portfolio.
findings.action: Decide early which of the walk-in, hood and gas service the new menu will use. Open the interceptor during due diligence to confirm its size before counting on it.

photos.alt: Stainless walk-in cooler with its door open, showing polymer shelving and a quarry tile floor
photos.caption: The walk-in cooler, off the rear of the kitchen.

findings.title: No rooftop units to inherit. The mall supplies the heating and cooling.
findings.body: As a ground-floor tenant under two more storeys, the unit has no rooftop plant of its own. Hydronic fan-coil units above the ceiling run off the mall's central water loop, so there is no packaged unit to replace at the end of its life. The ceiling void is about 5½ feet deep at the rear and well used by building services. Out front, the patio is about 610 square feet under a covered walkway, and the food-court side has an open servery about 8½ feet wide behind a roller shutter.
findings.action: Confirm the loop type and the capacity available to the unit with the landlord. Plan the ceiling routes early, because the void is shared with building services.

photos.alt: Looking up from the covered walkway at a glazed mall atrium and tan precast cladding against a blue sky
photos.caption: The open-air walkway on the patio side of the unit.

description: Two neighboring mall suites in Mission Viejo, CA surveyed for a combined café: power, cooling, water and shopfronts read from the plant itself.
kicker: Two-suite enclosed mall unit · Mission Viejo, California · Surveyed July 2026
h1: Two suites, two transformers, and a 480 V backbone already in place.
summary: A healthy fast-casual brand wanted to join two neighboring first-level suites in an enclosed regional mall in Mission Viejo into one store. One is a glazed corner unit, the other its next-door neighbor, both still trading on the day. The brand needed to know what each suite would bring to a combined fit-out, and what the fit-out would have to add. One visit, with both stores open, answered that.

findings.title: The two suites mirror each other electrically. Together they bring 75 kVA.
findings.body: Each suite takes a 480 V three-phase house supply and steps it down to 208Y/120 V through its own transformer, one 30 kVA and one 45 kVA. Combined, the new store inherits a 480 V backbone, about 75 kVA of step-down capacity, 480 V circuits for mechanical plant and room in the panels at both ends. The corner suite's back of house also holds a chilled stock room left from an earlier retail fit-out, with its own unit cooler overhead.
findings.action: Check the combined 75 kVA against the brand's equipment schedule before designing any new service, and plan the old chilled-store plant into the strip-out, since it is unlikely to suit the brand's walk-in.

photos.alt: Back-of-house store room with a ceiling-hung refrigeration unit cooler under a lay-in ceiling
photos.caption: The corner suite's store room, with the older chilled-store cooler overhead.

findings.title: A decorative corner front and a frameless glass one, joined by one wall.
findings.body: The corner suite has an ornate arched shopfront in painted timber frames, single-glazed behind the decoration. Its neighbor has a full-height frameless glass front with butt joints and a roller-shutter entrance. Between them is a short run of composite cladding that comes off easily. Behind the frontage, the wall between the suites runs full height to the deck, with about 14 feet clear to the underside of the steel.
findings.action: Treat the corner shopfront as part of the new storefront package and look at keeping the frameless glazing. Opening the dividing wall needs a fire-rated design and landlord approval, so start that conversation early.

photos.alt: Arched white timber shopfront frames and recessed downlights seen from inside the corner suite
photos.caption: The corner suite's arched shopfront frames, from the inside.

findings.title: Cooling from two different decades, and a food court overhead for water.
findings.body: Comfort cooling is a matched split system in each suite. The corner suite's dates from 2007 and runs on an older refrigerant. The neighbor's is a 2015 system, mid-life and serviceable. Domestic water comes in at half an inch, which is small for a café. But the mall's food court and its main restrooms sit almost directly above, so bigger water and drain connections are close at hand.
findings.action: Budget to replace the 2007 split, check the 2015 split for reuse against the combined layout, and agree upsized water and drainage with the landlord early.

photos.alt: Full-height frameless glass shopfront with track lighting and an entrance soffit
photos.caption: The neighboring suite: frameless glazing and the newer cooling system.

description: Two glazed units on an open-air concourse at Old Orchard, Skokie, surveyed to become one café: frontage, power, fire systems, water and storage.
kicker: Two-unit open-air retail space · Skokie, Illinois · Surveyed July 2026
h1: Two shopfronts, two ceiling heights, and a storage room bigger than the brief.
summary: A counter-service food and drink operator planned to combine two side-by-side glazed units on the open-air concourse at Old Orchard into one store, with a storage room off the service corridor behind. Both units were trading, and neither had any food-service fit-out left in place. The operator needed a clear picture of what the pair would give a first-time café fit-out and where the new work would sit. One visit, including the service level below, set that out.

findings.title: Thirty-eight feet of glass, with a 19-inch step in the ceiling.
findings.body: Together the two frontages give about 38 feet of continuous glazing onto a double-loaded, brick-paved concourse, broken only by a single stone pilaster. The units are a similar size but not a similar height: one has a drywall ceiling at 10 ft 0¼ in, the other a lay-in grid at 11 ft 7¾ in. The wall between them is a gypsum partition, and the roof joists run straight across it.
findings.action: Design the combined store around the ceiling step rather than against it, and confirm the dividing wall, the pilaster and the services crossing the wall against the base-building drawings before layout is fixed.

photos.alt: Clean white drywall ceiling with supply diffusers and flat panel lights in a retail unit
photos.caption: The lower of the two ceilings: clean drywall at just over 10 feet.

findings.title: Each unit has its own fire systems, so the fit-out doesn't wait on the neighbors.
findings.body: Each unit has its own fire alarm panel and its own sprinkler control valve inside its own space, both reporting back to the center. Nothing is shared with the unit next door. That means ceilings can be re-headed and alarm devices moved without arranging a shutdown of a system that serves other tenants. Power is split the same way: one unit has a 100 A service sized for small retail, the other 300 A.
findings.action: Build the electrical design around the 300 A unit, and confirm current inspection records for both units' fire systems at handover.

photos.alt: Red sprinkler control valve assembly with pressure gauge, tamper switch and drain on a block wall
photos.caption: A sprinkler control valve with tamper switch and drain, one of the center's distributed set.

findings.title: First-generation food service, with the big services already close by.
findings.body: Neither unit has a walk-in, a grease connection or a servery, so this is a first-generation food fit-out. The pieces it needs are nearby. A 2 in water main runs directly beneath the units, against a typical 1½ in requirement. Above-ground grease removal already operates elsewhere on the property, and the landlord was open to a grease room on the level below. The storage room off the rear corridor is far bigger than the roughly 300 sq ft asked for, with about 17 feet to the deck.
findings.action: Settle the grease route early, since it drives both cost and layout, and use the oversize storage room to take walk-in and dry storage off the trading floor.

photos.alt: Open-to-structure storage room with electrical panels and a sprinkler branch on a block wall
photos.caption: The storage room off the service corridor, open to the structure.

photos.alt: Block-walled rear service corridor with overhead piping and conduit
photos.caption: The rear service corridor that links the units to storage.

kicker: In-line retail unit · Gilbert, AZ · Surveyed June 2026
h1: A compact unit on a 480-volt building. The power was one step upstream.
description: A ~1,300 sq ft retail unit at SanTan Village, Gilbert, AZ, surveyed for a counter-service food operator: 480 V power, HVAC zoning and water.
summary: A counter-service food and drink operator was considering a compact in-line unit under the shaded walkways of SanTan Village. Their format runs on blenders, espresso and refrigeration, so it needs far more power than a retail shop, plus a second cooling zone and a good water supply. The unit was between tenancies, with a short-term pop-up inside. One visit showed how much of that the building could already give.

findings.title: A strong building service, with a suite supply sized for a shop.
findings.body: The building takes a 480Y/277 V three-phase service, and each suite is fed on its own breaker from a shared distribution board. This one runs through a 50 A feeder and a 30 kVA step-down transformer to a 100 A panel whose circuits were set up for retail lighting. That suits a shop. A food format with blenders, espresso machines and refrigeration needs more, and the transformer is what sets the limit.
findings.action: Upsize the suite feeder from the building board, swap the step-down transformer and panel for larger ones, and design new food-service circuits. The capacity sits one step upstream, so no new utility service is needed.

photos.alt: Open retail floor with a suspended ceiling, light timber-look flooring and a glazed storefront
photos.caption: The open front of house, about 1,170 sq ft in one room.

findings.title: One cooling zone today, and a simple way to make two.
findings.body: Cooling comes from a packaged rooftop unit that serves the whole building, with a single fan-powered VAV terminal over this suite. The terminal already carries its own electric reheat and runs on the building's automation system. The operator prefers at least two zones, and the open plan makes a second terminal straightforward.
findings.action: Add a matching fan-powered VAV terminal on the existing building controls, and confirm the rooftop unit's spare capacity with the landlord during design.

photos.alt: Aluminum storefront with double glass doors and stone-clad piers under a steel pergola
photos.caption: The recessed entry, shaded by the center's steel pergola.

findings.title: Water already sized for the format, and a clean deck overhead.
findings.body: A domestic cold-water line of at least 1½ inches, and possibly 2, runs the full width of the unit above the ceiling, which meets the operator's preference as it stands. The suite is sprinklered off the building's wet system, and an accessible restroom is already in place. Above the grid the structural deck is clean, so an open ceiling is an option.
findings.action: Confirm the water line size at fit-out, design new hot-water provision for the higher demand, and decide early whether to strip the ceiling back to the deck.

photos.alt: Restroom wall with a framed mirror, a stainless grab bar and an access panel for the water shut-off
photos.caption: The existing accessible restroom, with its own shut-off panel.

also: The storefront is about 17½ feet wide in two glazed bays around a recessed double door, with roughly 12 feet of height to work with inside. A misting system already serves the walkway outside, which could suit outdoor seating.
delivered: The client received a narrative condition and feasibility report with a nameplate-level equipment schedule, a brand-standards check and a 3D scan of the unit.

kicker: Second-generation restaurant unit · Palm Beach Gardens, FL · Surveyed July 2026
h1: Two frontages, three serving openings, and 800 amps already on the meter.
description: A ~3,300 sq ft restaurant unit at The Gardens Mall, Palm Beach Gardens, FL, surveyed for a fast-casual brand: 800 A service, patio and two frontages.
summary: A fast-casual brand growing in South Florida was weighing a vacant restaurant unit beside one of the main entrances to The Gardens Mall. It had been a full-service restaurant, with a cooking line the brand's counter format would never use. The real question was which parts of a well-built 2015 fit-out would carry over. One visit, and a drawing set from the scan, answered it.

findings.title: A front door on the mall and another on the forecourt.
findings.body: The unit faces two ways. Outside, a covered patio looks over the mall's landscaped forecourt and water feature, with a six-leaf bi-fold serving hatch onto a stone-topped counter, ceiling fans, festoon lighting and a gas fire pit. Inside, it fronts the main mall corridor with two bar-height glazed sectional doors and a pair of entrance doors. For a counter-service format, three ready-made serving openings across two frontages is a rare starting point.
findings.action: Plan the layout around the existing openings rather than new ones, and take up with the landlord the center-wide removal of the shopfront coving, which would raise the mall facade from 11 feet to over 13.

photos.alt: Covered patio with a steel-framed canopy, festoon lights and paved floor facing a landscaped forecourt with palm trees
photos.caption: The covered patio, looking out to the forecourt.

findings.title: More power and height than the format needs.
findings.body: The unit has a live 800 A service at 480/277 V three-phase, far more than a counter format draws. It feeds a main panel and two 208 V boards with plenty of spare ways, all scheduled and dated. Two 2015 rooftop units give about 23 tons of cooling across 3,300 square feet. The dining room is open to a metal deck at 16'8", and the back of house has close to 8 feet of ceiling void for new services.
findings.action: Run a load schedule against the existing boards and plan the fit-out as reuse and re-circuiting, not a service upgrade. Have the mechanical engineer confirm the rooftop units' remaining life before they are counted on.

photos.alt: Restaurant dining room open to an exposed metal deck, with booths and a glazed sectional serving door at the right
photos.caption: Open to the deck, with a glazed serving door onto the mall.

findings.title: The costly rooms are already built.
findings.body: Two restrooms from the 2014-15 fit-out, each with two stalls, are finished in large-format porcelain with stainless partitions and are fully accessible. A two-door walk-in cooler and freezer is structurally sound, and there is a commercial grease interceptor in the service yard. These are among the slowest and most expensive parts of a mall fit-out to build from scratch.
findings.action: Keep the restrooms and the walk-in boxes, fit new refrigeration to the boxes, and strip the previous cooking line, hoods and bar equipment the format doesn't use.

photos.alt: Restroom with brushed stainless toilet partitions, white tile and an accessible stall with grab bars
photos.caption: One of two accessible restrooms from the last fit-out.

also: Water comes in at 1½ inches off a 2-inch metered line, with a commercial triple-cartridge filtration head already plumbed. The gas service is capped at the meter position, with the internal riser still in place, so reinstating it is a utility request rather than new pipework.
delivered: The client received a narrative documentation report with a nameplate-level equipment schedule, a 3D scan, and a measured floor plan, reflected ceiling plan, interior and exterior elevations and Revit model drawn from it.
